# Why this note exists {.unnumbered}

The purpose is to build a durable measure-theory foundation for statistics,
not merely to decode one Bayesian paper. It makes expressions such as

$$
P(X\in A),\qquad \int h(x)P(dx),\qquad
\Pi(df\mid X_{1:n})
$$

feel like extensions of probability notation you already use. The same ideas
support probability models, expectations, asymptotics, stochastic processes,
survival analysis, and Bayesian priors.

## What this note assumes

This note assumes familiar probability, algebra, and basic calculus. It does
not assume a course in real analysis, abstract algebra, topology, or measure
theory.

Before continuing, read
[Sets, functions, inverse images, and pushforward distributions](sets-functions-and-pushforwards.qmd).
That prerequisite explains

- $\in$, $\subseteq$, unions, intersections, complements, and power sets;
- domains and codomains of functions;
- why $X^{-1}(B)$ is an inverse **image**, not necessarily an inverse function;
- exactly how $P_X=P\circ X^{-1}$ is evaluated.

When this note later introduces Lebesgue measure, densities, or
Radon-Nikodym derivatives, it supplies a short explanation and links to the
more detailed
[Lebesgue measure, integration, and densities](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd).

The central idea is simple:

> A measure assigns a nonnegative size to selected sets. A probability measure
> is a measure whose total size is one.

The technical structure tells us which sets may be assigned a size and which
maps may be treated as random variables.

# The three components of a measure space {#measure-space-components}

A **measure space** is a triple

$$
(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu).
$$

Each component has a different job.

| Object | Formal role | Probability interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| $\Omega$ | Underlying set | All elementary outcomes |
| $\mathcal F$ | Sigma-field of subsets of $\Omega$ | Events to which probability may be assigned |
| $\mu$ | Countably additive map $\mathcal F\to[0,\infty]$ | Size or mass of each measurable event |

The interval $[0,\infty]$ here means all nonnegative real numbers together
with the allowed value $+\infty$. A general measure may assign infinite size;
a probability measure never does because its total size is one.

The pair $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ is a **measurable space**. Adding a measure
produces a measure space. If $\mu(\Omega)=1$, then $\mu$ is a **probability
measure**, usually denoted by $P$, and $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability
space.

## Definition of a sigma-field {#sigma-field-definition}

A collection $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal P(\Omega)$ is a sigma-field if

1. $\Omega\in\mathcal F$;
2. $A\in\mathcal F$ implies $A^c\in\mathcal F$;
3. $A_1,A_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F$ implies
   $\bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty}A_j\in\mathcal F$.

These conditions imply that $\emptyset$, countable intersections, finite
unions, and set differences also belong to $\mathcal F$.

Here $\mathcal P(\Omega)$ is the **power set**, the collection of every subset
of $\Omega$. Therefore $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal P(\Omega)$ simply says
that every member of $\mathcal F$ is an event, although $\mathcal F$ need not
contain every conceivable subset.

On a finite or countable sample space we often can assign a measure to every
subset. On uncountable spaces such as $\mathbb R$, no translation-invariant
notion of length with the usual properties can be defined on every subset.
The sigma-field identifies a sufficiently rich, internally consistent collection
of measurable sets.

“Translation-invariant” means that moving a set left or right without changing
its shape should not change its length. The pathology behind nonmeasurable sets
is not needed for Walker; the practical point is that $\mu$ is defined on the
declared event collection $\mathcal F$, not automatically on every imaginable
subset.

The standard choice on $\mathbb R$ is the **Borel sigma-field**

$$
\mathcal B(\mathbb R)=\sigma\{(a,b):a<b\},
$$

the smallest sigma-field containing all open intervals.

The symbol $\sigma\{(a,b):a<b\}$ means “the sigma-field generated by the open
intervals.” It contains the intervals and everything that must be included to
obey the three sigma-field rules. You do not need to enumerate all of its
members. The detailed relation between Borel sets and Lebesgue-measurable sets
is explained in the [Lebesgue note](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd).
The optional
[generated-sigma-field note](generating-sigma-fields-and-pi-lambda.qmd#generated-sigma-fields)
develops generators, Dynkin systems, and the pi-lambda theorem for proofs and
uniqueness arguments.

## Definition of a measure {#measure-definition}

A function $\mu:\mathcal F\to[0,\infty]$ is a measure if

1. $\mu(\emptyset)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $A_1,A_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F$,

$$
\mu\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty}A_j\right)
=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\mu(A_j).
$$

The second property is **countable additivity**. It is the rule that makes
measurement compatible with limits.

Useful consequences include

- monotonicity: $A\subseteq B$ implies $\mu(A)\leq\mu(B)$;
- countable subadditivity:
  $\mu(\bigcup_j A_j)\leq\sum_j\mu(A_j)$;
- continuity from below: if $A_n\uparrow A$, then
  $\mu(A_n)\to\mu(A)$;
- continuity from above: if $A_n\downarrow A$ and $\mu(A_1)<\infty$, then
  $\mu(A_n)\to\mu(A)$.

The notation $A_n\uparrow A$ means

$$
A_1\subseteq A_2\subseteq\cdots,
\qquad
\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n=A,
$$

while $A_n\downarrow A$ means the sets shrink and their intersection is $A$.
These “continuity” properties say that measuring after taking the limiting set
agrees with taking the limit of the measurements.
Their derivation and their role in constructing measures are developed in
[Premeasures and measure extension](premeasures-and-measure-extension.qmd#measure-continuity).

# Familiar statistical models are measures {#statistical-models-as-measures}

## Bernoulli distribution

Let

$$
\Omega=\{0,1\},\qquad \mathcal F=\mathcal P(\Omega).
$$

For $0\leq p\leq1$, define

$$
P_p(A)=\sum_{x\in A}p^x(1-p)^{1-x}.
$$

Then $P_p(\{1\})=p$, $P_p(\{0\})=1-p$, and $P_p(\Omega)=1$.
The familiar probability mass function is a convenient way to specify the
probability measure $P_p$.

There is no need to enumerate every possible disjoint sequence to verify
countable additivity. Because the space has only two points, any disjoint
sequence contains at most two nonempty sets; additivity follows from the sum
defining $P_p$.

## Uniform distribution on $(0,1)$

Let the measurable space be $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Define

$$
P(A)=\int_A \mathbf 1_{(0,1)}(x)\,dx.
$$

This is a probability measure because

$$
P(\mathbb R)=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf 1_{(0,1)}(x)\,dx=1.
$$

Here $dx$ refers to Lebesgue measure. The function
$p(x)=\mathbf 1_{(0,1)}(x)$ is a density **relative to** Lebesgue measure.
The measure $P$, not the density by itself, is the probability distribution.

For now, read Lebesgue measure as ordinary length and read
$\mathbf 1_{(0,1)}(x)$ as 1 when $0<x<1$ and 0 otherwise. Thus the integral
measures the length of the portion of $A$ lying inside $(0,1)$. The
[Lebesgue note](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd) builds this
carefully from indicators and step functions.

# Random variables are measurable functions {#random-variables-measurable}

Suppose $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ describes the underlying experiment and
$(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)$ is a data space. A map

$$
X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathcal X
$$

is measurable if

$$
X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}\in\mathcal F
\quad\text{for every }B\in\mathscr X.
$$

This is the measure-theoretic definition of a random variable. It ensures that
the event $\{X\in B\}$ has a probability.

The inverse-image expression expands to

$$
X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.
$$

It asks which underlying outcomes produce values inside $B$. It does not claim
that $X$ has an inverse function. See the
[worked two-coin example](sets-functions-and-pushforwards.qmd#the-inverse-image-of-a-set)
if this distinction is not yet automatic.

## The distribution is a pushforward measure {#distribution-pushforward}

The distribution of $X$ is the probability measure $P_X$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)$ defined by

$$
P_X(B)=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr)=P(X\in B).
$$

This construction is called the **pushforward** of $P$ through $X$ and may be
written

$$
P_X=P\circ X^{-1}.
$$

The composition is evaluated on an output-space event $B$ as

$$
(P\circ X^{-1})(B)
=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr).
$$

Read from right to left:

1. $X^{-1}$ translates $B$ into an event in $\Omega$;
2. $P$ assigns that event a probability.

“Pushforward” means that the original probability law is now being expressed
in terms of values of $X$. Nothing is differentiated, multiplied, or assumed
to be one-to-one.

This distinction prevents a common notation confusion:

- $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ describes hidden elementary outcomes;
- $(\mathcal X,\mathscr X,P_X)$ describes the observable variable's
  distribution.

Statistical writing often works directly with $P_X$ and suppresses the
underlying $\Omega$.

# Integration unifies sums and continuous integrals {#measure-integration-summary}

For a measurable function $h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, its integral with
respect to a measure $P_X$ is written

$$
\int_{\mathcal X}h(x)\,P_X(dx).
$$

If $P_X$ is discrete with masses $p_j$ at points $x_j$, then

$$
\int h(x)P_X(dx)=\sum_j h(x_j)p_j.
$$

If $P_X$ has density $p$ relative to Lebesgue measure, then

$$
\int h(x)P_X(dx)=\int h(x)p(x)\,dx.
$$

Thus expectation is simply integration with respect to the distribution:

$$
E\{h(X)\}=\int h(x)P_X(dx).
$$

The starting identity behind a measure integral is

$$
\int\mathbf 1_A(x)P_X(dx)=P_X(A).
$$

Step functions become weighted sums of such probabilities, and general
integrable functions are obtained by approximation. This construction and the
meaning of $dx$ are developed in the
[integration note](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#integration-with-respect-to-a-measure).

The notation $P_X(dx)$ lets one formula cover discrete, continuous, and mixed
distributions. It does **not** require imagining a literal infinitesimal event.

# Densities depend on a reference measure {#reference-measure-densities}

A probability measure $P$ may have a density $p$ relative to a measure $\nu$.
The precise statement is

$$
P(A)=\int_A p(x)\,\nu(dx)
\quad\text{for every measurable }A.
$$

The Radon-Nikodym notation for the density is

$$
p=\frac{dP}{d\nu}.
$$

This notation is allowed when $P$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to**
$\nu$, written $P\ll\nu$. In plain language, every set to which $\nu$ assigns
zero must also receive zero from $P$. The
[density note](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#absolute-continuity-is-a-relationship-between-measures)
explains the condition, the Radon-Nikodym theorem, null sets, and mixed
distributions with examples.

Examples:

- a probability mass function is a density relative to counting measure;
- an ordinary continuous density is a density relative to Lebesgue measure;
- a point mass has no density relative to Lebesgue measure, but it is itself a
  perfectly valid probability measure.

This is why “distribution,” “measure,” and “density” should not be treated as
synonyms.

At the level needed here:

- a **distribution** is a probability measure;
- a **density** is a function representing that measure relative to a stated
  reference measure;
- the same measure-theoretic integral produces a sum for a PMF and an ordinary
  integral for a PDF.

# Bayesian analysis repeats the same pattern one level higher {#bayesian-higher-level}

In an ordinary probability model, $P$ measures subsets of the data space.
In Bayesian analysis, a prior $\Pi$ measures subsets of a parameter space.

If the unknown parameter is a density function, let $\mathcal D$ be a space of
candidate densities and let $\mathscr G$ be an appropriate sigma-field on
$\mathcal D$. Then

$$
(\mathcal D,\mathscr G,\Pi)
$$

is another probability space. Its “points” are whole functions. For a set
$A\in\mathscr G$,

$$
\Pi(A)=P(\text{the unknown density belongs to }A).
$$

This is one application of the general framework. The same move appears
whenever the unknown object is itself a function, distribution, regression
surface, or stochastic process.

# Check your understanding

You are ready to use measure notation in later statistical notes if you can
answer these questions.

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. In $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$, what is the domain of $\mu$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The domain is $\mathcal F$, the sigma-field of measurable subsets of $\Omega$.
Thus $\mu$ takes a **set** $A\in\mathcal F$ as input and returns a number in
$[0,\infty]$:

$$
\mu:\mathcal F\longrightarrow[0,\infty].
$$
:::

**2. What extra condition turns a measure into a probability measure?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Its total mass must be one: $\mu(\Omega)=1$. A probability measure is therefore
a measure with unit total mass and is usually denoted by $P$.
:::

**3. Why must a random variable be measurable?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For every permitted output event $B$, measurability guarantees that
$X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F$. The probability
$P(X\in B)=P\{X^{-1}(B)\}$ is then defined. Without measurability, some
output-space probability questions could pull back to sets to which $P$ cannot
assign a probability.
:::

**4. How does a distribution differ from one of its densities?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

A distribution $P$ is a measure that assigns probabilities to measurable sets.
A density $p=dP/d\nu$ is a function defined relative to a chosen reference
measure $\nu$ and satisfies

$$
P(A)=\int_A p\,d\nu.
$$

The same distribution can have different density formulas under different
reference measures, and some distributions have no density with respect to
Lebesgue measure.
:::

**5. What measure makes a PMF a density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Counting measure on the countable support. If $\#$ denotes counting measure,
then $p(x)=P(\{x\})$ and

$$
P(A)=\int_A p(x)\,\#(dx)=\sum_{x\in A}p(x).
$$
:::

**6. If the “points” of $\mathcal D$ are functions, what kinds of objects are
the events in $\mathscr G$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

They are measurable **sets of entire functions**, not sets of data values. For
example, an event could be the collection of all candidate densities whose mean
is positive, provided that collection belongs to $\mathscr G$. A prior $\Pi$
assigns probability to such collections.
:::

**7. Expand $(P\circ X^{-1})(B)$ without using the composition symbol.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$$
(P\circ X^{-1})(B)
=P\{X^{-1}(B)\}
=P\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.
$$

First pull $B$ back to an event in $\Omega$; then apply $P$ to that event.
:::
